insight.title: River Trout Harvest Energy From Turbulent Water
insight.subtitle: Instead of fighting rough currents, fish slalom through underwater eddies to propel themselves forward.
insight.notificationHook: River fish harvest energy from turbulence

sections.text: In fast-flowing rivers, trout hover almost effortlessly behind submerged rocks. They do not fight the crushing current. Instead, their bodies rhythmically curve and flex between the swirling eddies spinning off the obstacle.

As water splits around a stone, it forms a predictable street of rotating vortices. The trout senses these pressure waves and weaves between them, capturing the energy of each vortex to push itself forward.
By matching its rhythm to the spinning water, the fish achieves movement with almost zero muscular exertion. It turns chaotic, opposing fluid drag into a passive hydro-kinetic engine.
The water’s resistance becomes the fish’s momentum.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

China warned the United States on Friday against creating new export controls on computer chips. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning spoke at a regular press briefing. She said China opposes export control measures that disrupt global industrial chains. The warning follows a scandal involving Nvidia, the artificial intelligence chip company. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to an affair. He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at data center company Megaspeed. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department failed to add Megaspeed to a restricted list. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed to testify to the Senate Banking Committee on December tenth.

Turning to technology, OpenAI announced ChatGPT Wallet on Friday to let its AI agents buy items for users. The company built the payment feature with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa. Eligible users enter card information once and approve each purchase with a security check. Payment networks send the AI agent a token instead of real card details. Product lead Chaya Nayak said OpenAI is not taking a cut of purchases at the start. The tool is currently limited to Pro subscribers in the United States over eighteen years old. United Airlines and Amazon are currently blocking personal AI agents from making purchases on their platforms.

In housing news, United States existing home sales dropped to a sixteen-year low in October. The National Association of Realtors said sales fell eight point eight percent from last year. Sales of existing built units fell to three point seven five million. The median home sales price rose slightly to four hundred sixteen thousand seven hundred dollars. Sales declined in the Midwest, South, and West, while Northeast sales held steady. The average thirty-year mortgage rate currently sits at about seven point one eight percent. Federal Reserve interest rates sit between three point seven five percent and four percent. The central bank is expected to raise interest rates again next month.

Moving to global news, climate change could displace over two hundred billion people, according to the United Nations. Amy Pope leads the International Organization for Migration. She gave an interview at the climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. Pope said over two hundred billion people live in communities at risk of displacement. In 2025, extreme weather forced nearly thirty million people to flee their homes. Countries spend billions of dollars on border security while ignoring migration drivers, Pope stated. She estimated climate adaptation measures will cost about three hundred ten billion dollars. Current funding for adaptation measures stands at about thirty billion dollars.

In health news, lawmakers introduced legislation to curb financial conflicts on healthcare advisory boards. The bill targets members who serve on a preventive care panel. Reporting by STAT showed that some panel members could benefit financially from their decisions.

Finally, oil prices fell on Friday and are heading for a second weekly decline. President Donald Trump stated on Truth Social that a deal with Iran was not necessary. He indicated the United States will continue its blockade on Iranian oil shipments and trade sanctions. Brent crude futures dropped to ninety-five dollars and forty-one cents per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude dropped to eighty-eight dollars and fifty-two cents per barrel. Yemen's Houthis said they attacked a Saudi Arabian pipeline and an Aramco facility in Riyadh. Iran's military stated four oil tankers exploded in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. The Energy Information Administration reported United States crude inventories rose by four point seven million barrels.

Up next, a Microsoft outage disrupts global financial markets and forces traders onto phones.

A Microsoft software outage disrupted global financial markets and forced traders to use phones and faxes. Outlook, Teams, and Copilot services stopped working during a week of high market volatility. Rita Elkazzi, an execution-sales head at UBS Group, used alternative channels in Sydney. In Japan, the Finance Ministry could not receive emails due to the blackout. CMC Markets Singapore sales trader Eugene Koh said phone calls replaced instant email communications. Downdetector received about 200,000 reports of user issues during the outage. Microsoft shares dropped 0.4 percent in extended trading. Microsoft later said it saw positive results after restarting affected infrastructure.

Next, election outcomes in the United States are prompting Middle Eastern nations to re-evaluate their alliances. Iran's Middle East rivals plan to push for greater foreign and defense policy autonomy from America. This push follows the Democrats' sweeping victory in the midterm elections. The key regional partners include Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan.

Turning to South America, a digital bank collapse led to the removal of Paraguay's president. On November 2, Paraguay's central bank placed the digital bank Ueno into resolution. Regulators found Ueno's solvency ratio fell below half the legal minimum. A June 2026 report questioned about 146 million dollars in loans to related companies. Millions of customers lost access to their funds through the mobile app. President Santiago Peña resigned on November 5 after political pressure mounted. The Senate voted to strip Peña of immunity and place him under house arrest. Vice President Pedro Alliana took office to serve until 2028.

In business news, corporate records show financial links between tech giant Alibaba and chip buyer Megaspeed. Megaspeed faces scrutiny over potential unauthorized transfers of Nvidia artificial intelligence chips to China. Records show Megaspeed's Malaysian unit Speedmatrix pledged equipment to Singapore firm Apex Enterprise Solutions. Apex is ultimately owned by Alibaba Group Holding, according to corporate records. Short-seller Culper Research reported Alibaba sent funds through Apex to finance Megaspeed's chip purchases. Megaspeed owns seven subsidiaries across five overseas markets, according to 2024 statements. One subsidiary signed a 64.6 million dollar deal for data center land in August 2025. Speedmatrix received an Nvidia baseboard shipment on November 18, 2025.

In Europe, French politician Marine Le Pen prepares to present her political party's pension plans. The National Rally party wants to allow people who started working young to retire at 60. Le Pen pledged to repeal President Emmanuel Macron's reform that raises the retirement age to 64. She aims to save up to 155 billion dollars from France's budget by 2032. Le Pen says her pension changes would save up to 20 billion euros each year. France's public audit office says reversing Macron's reform could cost 10 billion euros annually. Pensions will reach 436 billion euros next year, representing 14 percent of economic output.

Finally, Polish President Karol Nawrocki vetoed a bill that would let regulators block online content. This decision marks his second rejection of legislation implementing the European Union Digital Services Act. Nawrocki stated that independent courts, not state officials, should decide if online content is illegal. The lower house of parliament passed the legislation in October following school knife attacks. Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski warned the veto leaves the nation without needed safety tools. Nawrocki has now vetoed 48 bills introduced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government. Minister Gawkowski told a press conference that he will draft a new bill on the issue.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

In fast-flowing rivers, trout hover almost effortlessly behind submerged rocks. They do not fight the crushing current. Instead, their bodies curve and flex between swirling eddies spinning off obstacles. When water splits around a stone, it forms rotating vortices. The fish senses these pressure waves and weaves between them. It captures the energy of each spinning vortex to push itself forward. By matching its rhythm to the water, the trout achieves movement with almost zero muscular exertion. The fish turns fluid drag into a passive kinetic engine. Water resistance becomes the fish's momentum. Where in your own life could you work with an obstacle instead of fighting it?

Thank you for listening to this edition of the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is our full analysis of the big stories making news right now.

Why is China warning the United States about computer chip exports right now? Beijing told Washington to stop adding trade limits after a scandal at chip maker Nvidia.

Computer chips are tiny electronic brains that power modern technology. Advanced chips are especially important for building artificial intelligence systems. The United States wants to maintain its lead in technology. So Washington created rules restricting exports of top computer chips to China. Nvidia is an American company that designs powerful artificial intelligence chips. Jensen Huang served as the chief executive officer of Nvidia for many years. President Donald Trump previously set limits on which Nvidia chips China could receive. Trump said China should not get any Nvidia chips above the H100 model. In December twenty twenty-five, Trump allowed H200 chips for approved Chinese customers. The United States government planned to take a percentage of those sales. Meanwhile, a data center business in Singapore named Megaspeed bought chips from Nvidia. Megaspeed secured more than four billion dollars of Nvidia chips. United States agents suspected Megaspeed of secretly smuggling some chips into China. Because of those concerns, Nvidia stopped all shipments to Megaspeed in June twenty twenty-five.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia on Thursday. He admitted to an affair with a former Megaspeed executive named Alice Huang. They are not related. United States officials suspect Alice Huang is a spy for China's intelligence service. About a year ago, President Trump was briefed on intelligence suggesting she was an asset. Trump decided not to do anything with that information at the time.

On Friday, China warned the United States against creating new computer chip export limits. Mao Ning, a spokesperson for China, said export controls disrupt global supply chains. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Nvidia's top chips may have reached China through Megaspeed. Bessent said there was a lot of leakage in the system. He criticized Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's agency for not blacklisting Megaspeed. The Entity List is the Commerce Department's blacklist that cuts companies off from American technology. Bessent said four federal agencies favored blacklisting Megaspeed for months. Reportedly, Bessent pressed Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Megaspeed. A Commerce spokesperson denied that conversation happened and said the departments work well together. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed to testify before a Senate committee on December tenth. Beijing rejected the spy claims and called them a pretext for a technology blockade.

Lawmakers in Washington are demanding tighter export controls after these leakage reports.

Bessent warns that technology leakage gives China an advantage in the artificial intelligence race. It is possible that Congress will push the Commerce Department to add Megaspeed to its blacklist.

Now, let us turn to a major shift in how artificial intelligence handles everyday online spending.

How will artificial intelligence software start buying products for you online? OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet so its digital assistants can make purchases for users.

OpenAI builds artificial intelligence tools, including the popular ChatGPT chatbot. The chatbot supports more than one point two billion active users every week. Nearly one hundred million of those people pay for monthly subscription accounts. In late September, OpenAI launched digital helpers called dots. People use these smart agents to handle daily tasks like managing personal calendars. OpenAI tried an instant checkout feature last fall, but quickly moved away from it. In March, the company updated its app to help users find and compare products online. Now OpenAI wants to help shoppers complete purchases through their digital helpers.

On Friday, OpenAI officially announced a new payment tool called ChatGPT Wallet.

OpenAI built the wallet alongside payment networks American Express, Mastercard, and Visa. The feature is launching first for adult Pro subscribers in the United States. Users add a payment card once and approve each purchase with a security check. Approval can use a fingerprint scan or Face ID. Payment networks issue temporary payment tokens for each transaction. The token contains a scoped card number, security code, and expiration date. The merchant and the AI agent never see the user's real card details. Cardholders keep their rewards and dispute protections for eligible purchases. Chaya Nayak at OpenAI told reporters the firm is not taking a cut of purchases yet. Luke Gebb at American Express said starting small lets them test the system safely. However, Visa tested twenty-two AI models as shoppers, and they failed almost forty-three percent of transactions. In addition, United Airlines announced it will block AI agents from booking tickets. Amazon also prevents AI agents from purchasing products on its platform. Banks like Schwab and JPMorgan are blocking AI agents from moving customer money. To help businesses, OpenAI published guidance explaining how websites can let agents through firewalls. OpenAI is also working with fraud prevention firms like Forter and payment processors like Stripe. Walmart is taking a different approach, allowing agents to shop using set spending limits.

Tech companies are rushing into automated commerce as more consumers try out personal digital agents.

Shopping features could eventually kickstart a new revenue stream for OpenAI. You can watch to see if major retail websites update their systems to welcome digital agents.

Next, we look at why buying a home in America has become so difficult recently.

Why did home sales in the United States drop to a sixteen-year low? High mortgage interest rates and rising inflation kept prospective buyers out of the housing market.

During the pandemic, average thirty-year mortgage interest rates fell to just above three percent. Lower borrowing costs made buying houses more affordable for many families. Later, overall inflation rose, which pushed the cost of living higher for everyday families. To fight inflation, the Federal Reserve began raising its key benchmark interest rate. Mortgage rates dropped below six percent in February twenty twenty-six before climbing again. Increasing inflation and higher interest rates amid the Iran war pushed mortgage rates back up.

On Wednesday, the National Association of Realtors released new housing data for October.

Sales of existing built homes dropped to three point seven five million units in October. That represents a fall of eight point eight percent compared to last year. Sales declined in the Midwest, South, and West, while sales in the Northeast held steady. The median sales price for existing homes rose slightly to four hundred sixteen thousand seven hundred dollars. Average thirty-year mortgage rates reached about seven point one eight percent. That is close to the twenty twenty-three peak of seven point seven nine percent. Lawrence Yun at the Realtors group said home buying is hard with rates this high. Yun noted that home sales fell to their lowest level since August twenty ten. Pending home sales, which measure signed contracts, reached their lowest level in history in September. Affordability and cost of living concerns played an outsized role in recent midterm elections. Those elections gave Democrats control of Congress next year. Census data shows growth in median rent outpaced inflation, while home ownership rates stagnated since twenty twenty-one. Economist Danielle Hale said shifting financial conditions and election uncertainties created a perfect storm for housing. Meanwhile, central bank interest rates sit in a range of three point seven five to four percent.

The Federal Reserve hiked rates in September, which pushed home loan costs back up as inflation rose.

High mortgage rates mean buying a house may remain expensive for many families. Watch for the central bank's next meeting, where officials could raise interest rates again next month.

Up next, climate change could force more than two hundred billion people from their homes.

Could extreme weather force billions of people away from their homes?

A United Nations official warned that climate change puts vast numbers of people at risk.

For many years, the climate on Earth has been changing. Rising heat creates stronger storms, ocean flooding, and longer droughts. These events destroy farmlands and ruin homes. When families lose their crops, they cannot feed themselves. They must leave their towns to find food and safety elsewhere. This movement of people across regions or borders is called migration.

To handle this, many countries focus on stopping people at their borders. They build fences and hire guards to keep migrants out. Governments spend billions of dollars every year on border security measures. However, border guards cannot stop bad weather or repair ruined farms. Border security only deals with people after they arrive.

The problem grew worse in twenty twenty-five. In that single year, severe weather forced nearly thirty million people to leave home. Those disasters included heavy storms, droughts, forest fires, extreme heat, and severe flooding.

Now, global officials are meeting at a United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Turkey. Amy Pope leads the International Organization for Migration. She gave an interview to the news agency AFP at the conference. Pope warned that over two hundred billion people live in communities at extreme risk. She said these people face a serious danger of being displaced.

Pope explained that helping communities protect themselves makes far more sense. She called climate adaptation measures a more humane and cost-effective solution. Estimates show that adaptation measures would cost about three hundred ten billion US dollars. However, governments have funded only about thirty billion US dollars so far. Pope stated that this funding is nowhere close to what is needed. She also regretted that many national heads of state skipped the talks.

Pope gave this warning right as leaders debated climate policy without full attendance. Some nations that worry most about migration chose not to attend the meeting. She wanted to show them that climate change and migration are connected.

If countries do not invest in adaptation, migration movements could increase significantly. Helping communities adapt may save human lives and lower future spending. Moving forward, we can watch if governments increase their climate adaptation funding. We can also watch if absent world leaders attend future climate conferences.

Now, let us turn to a story about healthcare rules in the United States.

United States lawmakers introduced new legislation to prevent financial conflicts of interest on healthcare advisory boards. This bill came after reporting by STAT showed that some panel members could benefit financially from their decisions. The proposed law aims to stop board members from gaining money based on official choices.

Next, we look at global oil prices and conflict in the Middle East.

Why are world oil prices falling even while conflicts continue in the Middle East?

Oil prices fell for a second week because the United States plans to keep blockading Iranian trade.

The United States and Israel have been involved in a war against Iran for nine months. Iran is a major oil producer, and the Middle East supplies crude around the world. The Strait of Hormuz is a vital waterway for shipping that crude oil.

To pressure Iran, the United States imposed economic sanctions and a trade blockade. These actions aim to prevent Iran from exporting its crude oil. At the same time, Iran supports regional armed groups, including Houthis in Yemen. These groups attack ships and energy facilities in neighboring countries.

Traders often worry that military conflicts will disrupt crude shipments. When crude oil supply falls, market prices usually jump higher. When supply remains stable, prices tend to ease downward.

Traders gained clearer information about future United States policy. United States President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that a deal with Iran was unnecessary. He indicated that he will stick with trade blockades and economic sanctions.

This statement helped drive oil prices down for a second consecutive week. Brent crude futures settled down slightly at ninety-five dollars and forty-one cents a barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude dropped to eighty-eight dollars and fifty-two cents a barrel. Over the week, Brent dropped two point four percent after falling sixteen percent the week before. West Texas Intermediate fell two point five percent after dropping thirteen percent previously.

Market analyst Chris Brankin at brokerage MiTrade noted that the oil market is priced to perfection. However, risks to shipping in the region remain high. Iran's military stated that four oil tankers exploded in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not independently confirm those reports. Yemen's Houthis also claimed attacks on a Saudi oil pipeline, a Red Sea facility, and Riyadh offices.

Meanwhile, United States crude inventories rose by four point seven million barrels last week. The Energy Information Administration reported total crude inventories reached four hundred fourteen point four million barrels.

Prices dropped because traders expect the blockade to lower chances of wider fighting. Rising fuel inventories in the United States also pushed market prices down.

Lower oil prices could mean cheaper energy costs for businesses and drivers globally. However, attacks on oil tankers mean unexpected supply cuts remain possible. Next, we can watch whether military events in the Strait of Hormuz reduce actual crude exports. We can also monitor future United States inventory reports to see if supplies keep rising.

Up next, a major Microsoft outage disrupts global financial markets and forces traders to use phones.

Why did financial traders around the world suddenly have to use phones and faxes?

A major software failure knocked out Microsoft services and disrupted global trading desks.

Traders used to call each other on landline phones to execute financial deals. Then financial firms built digital networks to speed up trading and manage daily operations. Microsoft became a major provider of software tools for these global markets. Banks relied heavily on Microsoft Outlook for email and Teams for workplace messaging. Firms also adopted Microsoft cloud services to store documents and run financial software online. This central technology helped thousands of financial institutions communicate quickly across borders. However, placing critical infrastructure in connected cloud data centers created new systemic risks. In September, a core authentication configuration issue caused a days-long Microsoft cloud outage. That incident demonstrated how connected software systems can interrupt major business operations worldwide.

On Thursday, a cascading software issue caused Microsoft data center servers to fail unexpectedly. The problems started in the Americas and quickly spread to servers across the globe. The outage knocked out Outlook email, Teams conferencing, and Copilot artificial intelligence tools. It also disrupted Defender security screening software and internal administrative control dashboards.

Downdetector recorded about 200,000 user issue reports during the widespread technical blackout. Traders rely heavily on instant messaging tools to negotiate asset prices and confirm daily transactions. When cloud servers fail, financial operations slow down because staff must verify details manually. In Australia, UBS execution-sales head Rita Elkazzi used alternative channels to confirm market trades. She noted that extra diligence was required to ensure trade recaps remained accurate. CMC Markets sales trader Eugene Koh said staff used phone calls and busy WhatsApp chats. BNP Paribas senior strategist Ryutaro Kimura reported trade confirmations backed up, creating settlement headaches. In Singapore, traders reported that some banks could not complete financial transactions. Indian firm IIFL Capital Services warned clients about delays in responding to email queries. Australia's main exchange operator ASX Ltd stated its bourse services remained fully operational. Truck manufacturer Workhorse Group Inc postponed its scheduled corporate earnings release. Japan's Finance Ministry lost email access due to disruptions on government shared IT platforms. Hedge fund manager Calvin Yeoh said he could not check reports or access trading platforms. Private wealth director Kenneth Goh relied on patchy phone calls while advising private clients.

Microsoft stated the outage involved a large number of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable. Company vice president Charles Lamanna said teams are reviewing how to prevent future issues. Microsoft reported there was no evidence of cyber attacks or malicious activity during the event.

Doug Madory from internet analysis firm Kentik reported traffic returned after 18 hours. Microsoft shares fell 0.4 percent in extended trading following the global service disruptions. Wilson Asset Management manager Matthew Haupt noted that some stock trading volumes fell. Market observers can watch if regulators demand stronger backup communication systems for financial firms.

Now, let's look at how recent election results could alter foreign policy across the Middle East.

United States election outcomes are prompting Middle Eastern nations to re-evaluate their alliances. Iran's Middle East rivals may accelerate their push for greater foreign and defense policy autonomy. This shift follows the Democrats' sweeping victory in the midterm elections. Key regional partners of the United States include Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan.

Next, let's turn to a banking crisis that quickly toppled a country's president from power.

How did a banking mobile app failure bring down a national president in just a few days?

A digital bank collapse triggered a political crisis that ousted Paraguay's president from power.

Paraguay spent years building an international image as a stable, low-tax business hub. The country drew investors through strong agricultural exports, hydroelectric power, and friendly commercial policies. Paraguay had attracted conservative foreign influencers who praised its low taxes and free market policies. In 2021, a new digital lender called Ueno launched to provide modern banking services. Ueno expanded rapidly by giving cash-back rewards and credit cards to lower-income citizens. In 2023, economist Santiago Peña was elected president of Paraguay. Peña previously served as a director at Banco Basa, a bank linked to former president Horacio Cartes. Peña appointed former banking partner Carlos Carvallo to head Paraguay's central bank. Peña also named Jorge Brítez to lead the state social security system, known as IPS. Under Brítez, IPS relaxed investment rules and placed massive cash deposits into Ueno. Ueno grew to manage about 850 million dollars in public funds. That included 355 million dollars from IPS, representing about nine percent of its portfolio. Meanwhile, tech firm ITTI, linked to Ueno's main owner Grupo Vázquez, won millions in state contracts.

In June 2026, regulators found roughly 146 million dollars in loans linked to Ueno's main shareholder. On November second, the central bank placed Ueno into resolution due to severe solvency problems. The bank shut down transactions, locking nearly three million customers out of their money.

Protesters immediately flooded streets near Congress, accusing government leaders of stealing their savings. Central bank president Carlos Carvallo resigned on November third and faces criminal corruption charges. President Santiago Peña resigned on November fifth as the political scandal grew. Reporters previously revealed Peña held a 1.58 percent stake in Ueno Holding until 2025. The Senate voted unanimously to remove Peña from office and stripped his immunity. Peña was placed under house arrest and charged with corruption crimes, though he denies wrongdoing. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president to serve until 2028.

The central bank acted after Ueno's solvency ratio fell below half the legal minimum limit. Supervisors had warned earlier about unbacked loans given to companies tied to bank insiders. The regulator finally stopped operations when accounting adjustments revealed that Ueno could not cover its risks.

The crisis cracks Paraguay's reputation as a stable regional destination for foreign capital. Under President Peña, the country aligned closely with United States regional economic strategy. On October 23, Paraguay signed the Pax Silica Declaration covering critical minerals and computing infrastructure. Before the collapse, the International Monetary Fund projected economic growth of 4.4 percent for 2026. That followed solid growth of 6.6 percent achieved in 2025. Moody's and S&P had also upgraded Paraguay's debt to investment grade status. Investors can watch whether prosecutors uncover broader corruption involving public pension deposits in private banks.

Next, we examine how a financing link between Alibaba and Megaspeed was traced through Singapore and Malaysia.

How did a Chinese technology giant get linked to a company buying restricted computer chips? Official records reveal a Singapore firm owned by Alibaba made a deal with a unit of Megaspeed.

Let us start from the beginning to see how this story unfolded. The United States placed export restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips. They created these rules to limit China's access to powerful computing technology. A firm named Megaspeed made massive purchases of these advanced chips from Nvidia. Because Megaspeed bought so many chips, United States authorities began investigating the firm in late 2024. They suspected Megaspeed of breaching export rules by sending restricted chips to China. 

Megaspeed operates seven subsidiaries across five overseas markets. Three of those subsidiaries are located in Malaysia. One Malaysian unit is called Speedmatrix, which operates cloud-hosting services. Another unit named MSFusion agreed to buy land in Johor for a proposed data centre. Megaspeed also owns businesses in Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. 

Meanwhile, a company called Apex was incorporated in Singapore in July 2023. Apex operates from an address leased by Alibaba and its shopping unit, Lazada. Records show Apex is owned by Cloud Intelligence Cayman Holding. Its ultimate parent company is Alibaba Group Holding, incorporated in the Cayman Islands. Apex described its business as providing procurement activities in its 2025 financial report. Former director Yuan Qian matches the Chinese name of a former Alibaba executive, Selina Yuan. 

In June 2024, Speedmatrix pledged its network equipment and intellectual property rights to Apex. This agreement gave Apex security over those assets if Speedmatrix failed contractual duties. In May, research firm Culper Research published a report about this financial connection. Culper Research held a position that profited if Nvidia's share price fell. The report alleged Alibaba channelled billions through Apex to fund Megaspeed's chip purchases. 

What changed recently is that reporters reviewed corporate records from Malaysia. Records show the financial deal between Apex and Speedmatrix remained active on November 11, 2026. Shipping records show Speedmatrix received Nvidia baseboards as recently as November 18, 2025. Singapore police confirmed in October 2025 that they were investigating Megaspeed for domestic law breaches. Reporters visited the registered address of Swiftdata, the firm that owns Megaspeed. An interior design firm was there and denied knowing Swiftdata or Megaspeed. 

Scrutiny grew further in late October 2026 over ties between two key leaders. Those leaders were Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and former Megaspeed director Alice Huang. On November 8, Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, and he resigned on November 12. 

Why is this happening right now? Governments are increasing pressure to trace high-tech supply chains around the world. On November 12, Megaspeed stated it hired a law firm to check its chip inventory. This matters because global trade rules are being tested by complex corporate networks. Watch whether law enforcement agencies find evidence of illegal chip transfers.

Now let us travel to Europe for our next story.

How is a French political party trying to balance early retirement promises with government spending? Marine Le Pen's party is adjusting its pension plans to calm nervous financial investors. 

Let us look at how France got to this point. Pensions are by far the single biggest public expense in France. Next year, pensions will reach 436 billion euros, which equals 14 percent of economic output. France uses a pay-as-you-go system, where current workers fund current retirees. In 2023, President Emmanuel Macron passed an unpopular overhaul. His reform aimed to gradually raise the retirement age to 64 from 62. That change caused months of public protests across the country. The government suspended the plan last year to secure parliamentary backing for its budget. 

Marine Le Pen leads the far-right National Rally party. Older voters represent a key group of supporters for her party. She promised to cancel Macron's reform and let young starters retire at age 60. Le Pen also said she would save 140 billion euros by 2032. However, economists and investors doubt those spending cuts are achievable. Reversing Macron's reform could cost 10 billion euros every single year. 

What changed is that elections are approaching in five months. Opinion polls suggest the National Rally could take power in five months' time. Because investors are nervous about public debt, the party is revealing its detailed numbers. Party president Jordan Bardella said none of the past reforms fixed the system properly. The party will present its new pension plans next Tuesday. 

Under the updated plan, contribution years will matter more than a single retirement age. Workers would need between 40 and 42 years of contributions for a full pension. Party spokesman Jean-Philippe Tanguy said workers retiring at 62 without full contributions face reduced benefits. This means people who attend higher education might still need to work into their mid-60s. Bardella also proposed creating incentives for employers to retain older workers. Additionally, workers could put some contributions into a sovereign wealth investment fund. 

Why is this happening right now? The party must convince financial markets that its economic plans are realistic before the vote. This matters because pension rules directly shape the financial futures of millions of French citizens. Watch whether investors accept these modified promises when the full plan is presented next week.

Next, we turn to a debate over internet safety and free speech in Poland.

Why did Poland's president block a proposed law targeting dangerous online posts? President Karol Nawrocki vetoed the bill because he felt it gave officials too much control over speech. 

Let us look at the history behind this ongoing political fight. The European Union set internet safety rules called the Digital Services Act. Member countries must pass their own national laws to enforce these rules locally. In Poland, executive power is split between political rivals. President Karol Nawrocki is an ally of the nationalist opposition party. Prime Minister Donald Tusk leads a pro-European coalition government. These leaders have clashed repeatedly since Nawrocki took office. In fact, President Nawrocki has vetoed 48 of the government's bills. 

Nawrocki first vetoed a digital content bill in January. After that rejection, the Sejm, Poland's lower house of parliament, passed a narrowed bill in October. The bill allowed regulators to order the blocking of criminal threats and violent incitement. Citizens could appeal those online content blocks in independent courts. Urgency grew after a string of knife attacks at Polish schools in October. In one attack, a 15-year-old wore a helmet-mounted camera to record the violence. 

What changed today is that President Nawrocki vetoed this revised bill on Friday. In a video on X, Nawrocki said officials should never decide if content is criminal. He stated that ruling on crimes is solely the job of independent courts. He accused the government of using school tragedies to gain arbitrary control over public speech. 

Government officials reacted with strong anger to the president's veto. Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the veto leaves Poland without tools against online hate. Prime Minister Tusk posted that protecting children from online criminals should unite all politicians. 

Why did this conflict happen right now? The government wanted quick powers to stop online violence following the recent school attacks. This matters because democracies everywhere struggle to balance online safety with free expression. Minister Gawkowski stated he will draft another version of the legislation. Watch to see if parliament can construct a bill that survives another presidential veto.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

In fast-flowing rivers, trout can stay in place behind sunken rocks with almost no effort. You might think the heavy current would wash them away. Instead of fighting the strong water, the fish uses the river's own strength. When fast water hits a stone, it splits into spinning circles called vortices. These swirling eddies form a predictable path behind the rock. 

The trout senses pressure waves in the water with its body. It then curves and flexes rhythmically between the rotating vortices. By weaving through these spinning currents, the trout captures energy from the moving water. This kinetic energy actually pushes the fish forward. The trout matches its body rhythm directly to the swirling water around it. Because of this matching rhythm, the fish moves using almost zero muscle effort. It turns fluid drag into a working engine powered by the river itself. 

The natural resistance of the water becomes the momentum that propels the fish. This is a fascinating trick of nature. Instead of pushing harder against a force, the trout works alongside that same force. It finds power inside the very obstacles that seem to block its path. Think about the challenges or friction you face in your daily routine. Where in your life could you stop fighting the current and let resistance carry you forward?

Thank you for spending time with Sift In-Depth. Until next time, keep looking deeper into the stories around you.
